a: because of what was shown them in the creatures sent against them
t: What was shown, or how ugly?
p: Vaticanus has a word meaning "shown"; Ephraemi has "loathsomeness," which the KJV follows ("the ugly sight").

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), Swete's text; the Old Latin in the Vulgate ("the things that were shown and sent among them")
readings.en: because of the [thing] shown of those sent upon them
readings.plain: because of what was shown them in the creatures sent against them

readings.w: Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus (C, 400s AD), as Swete reports; KJV ("the ugly sight of the beasts sent among them")
readings.en: because of the loathsomeness of those sent upon them
readings.plain: because of how loathsome the creatures sent against them were

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text, which the Latin supports. Vaticanus's participle has no noun of its own; Ephraemi's noun, which differs by a few letters, reads more smoothly. The meaning is close either way.
b: Swete also reports that Vaticanus itself was garbled here: its first hand wrote διχθ-, which a corrector changed to δειχθ-, Swete's text. The first hand of Sinaiticus has χθεισαν, and an early corrector of Sinaiticus διχθ-.

a: a token of salvation
t: Token, or counsel?
p: Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read συμβουλον, a word of the "counsel" family, where Vaticanus has σύμβολον, "token."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; the Latin Vulgate (signum habentes salutis, "having a sign of salvation"); KJV ("a sign of salvation")
Codices Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Alexandrinus (A), as Swete reports them (page 634 of his second volume)

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text, which the Latin and the KJV support. The two words differ by one letter. συμβουλον belongs with σύμβουλος, "counselor, adviser" (the word of Romans 11:34); with it the bronze snake becomes God's advice for their rescue, close in sense to the "reminder" of the next line.
b: In the same line Swete reports that Alexandrinus has νομον for νόμου ("the commandment, the law") and that Sinaiticus leaves out "your."

a: which heals all things
t: Heals all things, or can do all things?
p: A corrector of Sinaiticus changed "heals" to "is able"; Alexandrinus and Ephraemi have "heals everyone."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; Sinaiticus (ℵ) first hand
Codex Sinaiticus, corrector (ℵ c.a)
readings.en: the one able [to do] all things

readings.w: Codices Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD) and Ephraemi (C)

why: Vaticanus and the first hand of Sinaiticus agree, and "heals" fits the healing story.

a: You sent them bread from heaven
t: Sent, or provided?
p: Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi read "you provided them from heaven," the wording the Latin follows.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; KJV ("didst send them from heaven")
readings.en: bread to them from heaven you sent
readings.plain: You sent them bread from heaven

readings.w: Codices Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A) and apparently Ephraemi (C); the Latin Vulgate (paratum panem de cælo præstitisti illis)
readings.en: bread from heaven you provided them
readings.plain: You provided them with bread from heaven

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text. The meaning hardly changes. The Latin verb praestitisti, "you provided," matches παρέσχες rather than ἔπεμψας, and the Latin line is the one that entered the liturgy of Corpus Christi (see the note on this verse).

a: their enemies' crops
t: Enemies or nations?
p: Alexandrinus reads "the nations" instead of "the enemies."

readings.w: Codices Vaticanus (B), Sinaiticus (ℵ), Ephraemi (C); Swete's text; KJV
Codex Alexandrinus (A)

why: The other great codices agree, and "enemies" matches 16:8.

a: as the daylight rises
t: At dawn, or before dawn?
p: A corrector of Sinaiticus reads "before the rising of the light."

readings.w: Codices Vaticanus (B), Alexandrinus (A), Ephraemi (C); Sinaiticus first hand; Swete's text; KJV ("at the dayspring"); Latin (ad ortum lucis)
Codex Sinaiticus, corrector (ℵ c.a)
readings.en: before the rising of the light

why: Most witnesses agree. The corrector's reading repeats the first line's idea of getting ahead of the sun.

a: scattered
t: Scattered or darkened?
p: Alexandrinus and Ephraemi read "they were darkened" instead of "they were scattered."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; Sinaiticus (ℵ) with a compound of the same verb; KJV; Latin (dispersi sunt)
Codices Alexandrinus (A) and Ephraemi (C)

why: The two Greek words differ by a letter or two. "Darkened" fits the darkness plague and may be an easier reading made by a copyist; Vaticanus, Sinaiticus and the Latin agree on "scattered."

a: Noises boomed all around and shook them
t: Noises that shook them, or noises crashing down?
p: Vaticanus's first hand has noises that "shook" them; a corrector of Vaticanus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi have noises "crashing down."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), first hand; Swete's text
readings.plain: Noises boomed all around and shook them

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, corrector (B ab), Codices Alexandrinus (A) and Ephraemi (C); compare the Latin (sonitus descendens, "a noise coming down") and the KJV ("noises as of waters falling down")
readings.plain: Noises came crashing down all around them

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ)
readings.plain: Noises boomed all around and troubled them

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text. The reading "crashing down" has three witnesses and may lie behind the Latin "a noise coming down" and the KJV's "falling down." Either way the Egyptians are surrounded by noise.
b: In the same verse Swete reports that Alexandrinus and Ephraemi read αφοβους and διεφυλαττεν in the first line (the sense is the same), and that Alexandrinus has μυθος, "story," for μυχός, "inner room," a slip of one letter.

a: testifies by itself that it is a coward
t: By itself, or by its own witness?
p: A corrector of Sinaiticus adds "its own," and Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus spell the verb μαρτυρι, which can be read as "witness": hence the KJV's "condemned by her own witness."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text
readings.orig: δειλὸν γὰρ ἰδίως πονηρία μαρτυρεῖ καταδικαζομένη
readings.en: for wickedness, being condemned, testifies peculiarly [that it is] cowardly
readings.plain: testifies by itself that it is a coward

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, corrector (ℵ c.a), who adds ιδιω, "its own"; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus spell the verb μαρτυρι; KJV ("condemned by her own witness, is very timorous")
readings.en: for wickedness, condemned by its own witness, [is] cowardly
readings.plain: is a coward, condemned by its own witness

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text. Swete lists μαρτυρι as a spelling of the verb μαρτυρεῖ, "testifies," but with the corrector's added "its own" the same letters read as "by its own witness," which is how the KJV took them. Both readings say that a guilty conscience condemns itself.

a: because they had not suffered too
t: Had not suffered, or had suffered?
p: Vaticanus reads "then" (οὖν), Alexandrinus "not" (οὐ). The Plain English Translation follows Alexandrinus, with the Latin and the KJV.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A); the Latin Vulgate (quia non et ipsi eadem passi erant); KJV ("because they also had not suffered the same things")
readings.en: that they too had not suffered
readings.plain: because they had not suffered too

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text
readings.en: that, then, they too had suffered

why: This is a departure from Swete's text. Vaticanus's οὖν differs from Alexandrinus's οὐ by one letter, and without "not" the line gives a strange sense (the Egyptians calling Israel blessed for suffering). The Latin, made from an early Greek copy, has "not."
b: The Latin also differs at the end: "they glorified you" instead of "they called them blessed."

a: the divine law
t: Divine law, or law of holiness?
p: Sinaiticus reads "the law of holiness"; the Latin has "the law of justice."

readings.w: Codices Vaticanus (B), Alexandrinus (A); Swete's text; KJV ("a holy law")
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ)
Latin Vulgate (justitiae legem); Douay ("a law of justice")

why: Vaticanus and Alexandrinus agree. Sinaiticus's word fits the "holy children" of the same verse and may come from them.

a: And already the fathers were leading the songs of praise.
t: The fathers singing, or singing of the fathers?
p: In Vaticanus the fathers lead the praise; in Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and the Latin the people sing the fathers' praises.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; KJV ("the fathers now singing out the songs of praise")
readings.plain: And already the fathers were leading the songs of praise.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, corrector, and Codex Alexandrinus (A) read προαναμελποντες; the Latin (patrum jam decantantes laudes); Douay ("singing now the praises of the fathers")
readings.en: already singing first the praises of the fathers
readings.plain: And already they were singing the fathers' songs of praise.

why: The Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus. The difference is one ending: in Vaticanus "the fathers" (the heads of families, or the patriarchs) lead the hymns; in the other reading the people sing songs handed down from their fathers.

a: the crowd
t: Crowd, disturbance, destroyer or wrath?
p: Every Greek codex has "the crowd." The Latin has "crowds," the KJV "the destroyer," and the NRSVUE corrects it to "wrath."

readings.w: The Greek codices that Swete reports, with no variant here; Swete's text
The Latin Vulgate; Douay ("the disturbance")
KJV ("So he overcame the destroyer")
NRSVUE, which prints "wrath" and marks it as a correction of the Greek ("Cn: Gk multitude")

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the Greek that the codices have. "The crowd" is hard to place, which is why translators reach for other words; the KJV's "destroyer" and the NRSVUE's "wrath" fit the plague but are not what the Greek says, and the NRSVUE marks its word as a correction.

a: these were what they feared
t: They feared, or it feared?
p: Vaticanus has a plural verb; a corrector of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus have the singular, "it feared," with the destroyer as subject.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text
Codex Sinaiticus, corrector (ℵ c.a), Codex Alexandrinus (A); Latin (haec extimuit); KJV ("and was afraid of them")

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete. The plural may mean the destroyer and its forces; the singular makes the destroyer alone the subject. The sense is the same: the priest's robe and prayer turned back the plague.

a: turned around so your people could leave
t: Turned around, or gave leave?
p: Vaticanus says the Egyptians "turned around"; a corrector of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus say they "allowed" Israel to go.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; Sinaiticus's first hand has the same word spelled επεστρεψαντες, and a later hand apparently restored επιστρ.
readings.plain: turned around so your people could leave

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, corrector (ℵ c.a), and Codex Alexandrinus (A); the Latin Vulgate (cum ipsi permisissent ut se educerent); KJV ("having given them leave to depart")

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text. The two words differ by one letter (σ). In Vaticanus the Egyptians reverse their earlier refusal; in the other reading they give permission. "Allowed" is the easier sense, which a copyist could have reached by dropping one letter.

a: would make a journey beyond belief
t: Experience the journey, or cross by it?
p: Vaticanus reads "experience" (πειράσῃ); a corrector of Vaticanus and Alexandrinus read "cross" (περάσῃ).

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B) first hand, Swete's text
readings.plain: would make a journey beyond belief

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, corrector (B ab), Codex Alexandrinus (A); KJV ("might pass a wonderful way"); Latin (mirabiliter transiret)
readings.plain: would cross over by a road beyond belief

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete. The words differ by one letter; "cross" fits the sea crossing, "experience" fits the idea of a trial survived.

a: obeying the commands meant for it
t: Its own commands, or your commands?
p: Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read "your commands"; Vaticanus, followed by the KJV, has "its own commands."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; KJV ("serving the peculiar commandments that were given unto them")
readings.plain: obeying the commands meant for it

readings.w: Codices Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Alexandrinus (A); Latin (deserviens tuis praeceptis)

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete. "Its own" may echo "its own kind" in the same line; "your" is the plainer reading. Either way the commands are God's.

a: their rescuer
t: Who rescues, or who rescued?
p: Alexandrinus and Ephraemi read a past tense, "who had rescued them," which the KJV follows.

readings.w: Codices Vaticanus (B) and Sinaiticus (ℵ), Swete's text
Codices Alexandrinus (A) and Ephraemi (C); KJV ("who hadst delivered them")

why: The Plain English Translation follows Vaticanus and Sinaiticus.

a: not without the signs that had taken place
t: Signs that had taken place, or signs beforehand?
p: Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi read "signs that had come before," which the KJV and the Latin follow.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text
readings.en: not without the signs that had happened
readings.plain: not without the signs that had taken place

readings.w: Codices Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), Ephraemi (C); KJV ("not without former signs"); Latin (non sine illis quae ante facta erant argumentis)
readings.en: not without the signs that had happened beforehand
readings.plain: not without the signs that had taken place beforehand

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text. Vaticanus's "had taken place" already points back to signs given before the punishment, so the two readings say nearly the same thing; the other three codices and the Latin make "before" explicit with the prefix προ-. A copyist could have added the prefix to make the sense plain or dropped it by accident, and the evidence does not settle which, so the Plain English Translation keeps its base text.

a: Fire in water was stronger than its own power
t: Stronger than itself, or forgetting itself?
p: Alexandrinus and Ephraemi add "forgetting," giving the KJV's "forgetting his own virtue."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; Latin (ignis in aqua valebat supra suam virtutem)
readings.orig: πῦρ ἴσχυσεν ἐν ὕδατι τῆς ἰδίας δυνάμεως
readings.en: fire was strong in water beyond its own power
readings.plain: Fire in water was stronger than its own power

readings.w: Codices Alexandrinus (A) and Ephraemi (C) (Sinaiticus shares their ἴσχυεν, "had power," but not the added word); KJV ("The fire had power in the water, forgetting his own virtue")
readings.orig: πῦρ ἴσχυεν ἐν ὕδατι τῆς ἰδίας δυνάμεως ἐπιλελησμένον
readings.en: fire had power in water, having forgotten its own power
readings.plain: Fire had power in water, forgetting its own nature

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text with the Latin. The added word repeats the "forgot" of the next line.
b: In the second line Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi read φύσεως, "nature," for δυνάμεως, "power": water forgot its quenching "nature" (so the KJV and the Latin). The meaning is the same.
